facts.statement: Ozarcus was an extinct genus of symmoriiform cartilaginous fish that lived during the Carboniferous period in Arkansas.
facts.quote: Ozarcus is an extinct genus of symmoriiform cartilaginous fish from the Carboniferous period of Arkansas.

facts.statement: The genus name Ozarcus honors the Ozark Mountains where it was found, and the species name mapesae honors its discoverer G. K. Mapes.
facts.quote: The genus is named after the Ozark Mountains (the region of discovery) while the species was named after its discoverer, G. K. Mapes.

facts.statement: The holotype fossil, a warped but three-dimensionally preserved skull with gill baskets discovered by G. K. Mapes, is cataloged as AMNH FF20544.
facts.quote: The holotype fossil, AMNH FF20544 (formerly labelled as OUZC 5300), was a warped yet three-dimensionally-preserved skull with gill baskets that was discovered by G. K. Mapes.

facts.statement: A partial braincase previously identified as Cobelodus and described in 2007 was reclassified as Ozarcus in 2017.
facts.quote: A partial braincase (FMNH PF 13242) from the same site, previously been referred to Cobelodus and described in detail in 2007, was referred to Ozarcus in 2017.

facts.statement: Ozarcus possesses branchial arches that show unexpected similarities to bony fish rather than typical cartilaginous fish.
facts.quote: Ozarcus has branchial arches (bones of the gill basket) with unexpected similarities to osteichthyans (bony fish) rather than chondrichthyans (cartilaginous fish).

facts.statement: Unlike modern sharks, the first four branchial arches of Ozarcus have two pairs of pharyngobranchials that form a solid roof over the gill cavity, a condition similar to bony fish.
facts.quote: Unlike modern chondrichthyans, the first four branchial arches have two pairs of pharyngobranchials which bend forwards to form a solid roof to the gill cavity, conditions akin to the two sets (infra- and supra-pharyngobranchials) of osteichthyans.

facts.statement: Ozarcus was initially tentatively classified within the family Falcatidae due to its small teeth resembling those of Falcatus and Damocles.
facts.quote: The initial description of Ozarcus tentatively placed it as a member of the family Falcatidae, based on its small teeth similar to Falcatus and Damocles.

facts.statement: Later research repositioned Ozarcus as a sister taxon to Dwykaselachus or near the base of Symmoriiformes, separating it from the falcatid Damocles.
facts.quote: In contrast, later papers placed Ozarcus (represented by specimen FMNH PF 13242) as the sister taxon to Dwykaselachus or close to the base of Symmoriiformes, far away from the falcatid Damocles.

facts.statement: Ozarcus lived during the Serpukhovian stage, approximately 330.3 to 326.9 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Serpukhovian to Serpukhovian (330.3 to 326.9 million years ago)

rejected.statement: The type species Ozarcus mapesae was named in 2014 based on cartilaginous skulls found in the Serpukhovian-age Fayetteville Formation.
rejected.quote: The type species, Ozarcus mapesae, was named in 2014 based on cartilaginous skulls from the Serpukhovian-age Fayetteville Formation.
